name: Li-Fraumeni syndrome
aliases: sarcoma, breast, leukaemia and adrenal gland (SBLA) syndrome

reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with very high lifetime cancer risk
The core tumour spectrum comprises soft-tissue and osteosarcomas, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma and leukaemia, often with childhood or early-adult onset
Suspect the syndrome when there are multiple primary tumours in one individual, cancers at unusually young ages, or clustering of the characteristic tumours across generations
Paediatric adrenocortical carcinoma and choroid plexus carcinoma are near-pathognomonic and warrant TP53 testing regardless of family history
Intensive whole-body MRI surveillance (Toronto protocol) with breast MRI, brain imaging and biochemical monitoring is the cornerstone of early detection
Therapeutic radiotherapy is used cautiously because of the risk of radiation-induced second malignancies in TP53 carriers
Classic and Chompret criteria guide who should be offered germline testing, but many carriers fall outside strict clinical criteria
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome results from a heterozygous germline loss-of-function variant in TP53, the gene encoding the p53 protein that acts as a master regulator of the cellular response to DNA damage. Normally p53 arrests the cell cycle to permit repair or triggers apoptosis when damage is irreparable, so its impairment allows cells carrying genomic damage to survive and proliferate. Loss or mutation of the remaining wild-type allele in somatic tissue removes this checkpoint entirely, producing genomic instability and driving the diverse, early-onset tumours characteristic of the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Neurofibromatosis type 1 with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours
Sporadic early-onset breast cancer without an identifiable germline cause
Familial adenomatous polyposis presenting with childhood brain tumours
additionalInvestigations: Germline TP53 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, ideally within a multigene cancer panel
Whole-body MRI as part of a structured surveillance protocol
Annual breast MRI in adult female carriers
Dedicated brain MRI and clinical neurological review
Abdominal ultrasound and biochemical adrenal screening in children
Detailed multigenerational pedigree assessment against classic and Chompret criteria
redFlags: Multiple primary malignancies in a single individual, especially with early onset
Childhood adrenocortical carcinoma or choroid plexus tumour
A new mass or persistent symptom in a known carrier suggesting a further primary cancer
Radiation-field second malignancy after prior therapeutic irradiation
reference.prognosis: Carriers face a very high cumulative lifetime cancer risk, frequently developing more than one primary tumour, and childhood-onset disease is common. Structured surveillance improves early detection and survival, but the diversity and aggressiveness of tumours mean prognosis remains guarded and lifelong monitoring is required.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because family history is limited, since de novo variants and incomplete pedigrees are frequent
Using therapeutic radiotherapy without weighing the heightened risk of radiation-induced tumours
Overlooking a second primary by attributing new symptoms solely to a prior cancer
Failing to offer cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
